title: It's All Over
speaker: Ryushin Andrea Thach
summary: Ryushin Andrea Thach's main teaching emphasizes that death and dying are not something to be feared, but rather a natural part of life, and that living in the present moment is what truly matters. From a Soto Zen perspective, life only exists because of death, and true appreciation for life comes from embracing its impermanence. This understanding allows us to see that everything is interconnected and that separation is an illusion, enabling us to experience a deeper sense of oneness and acceptance in the present moment.

It's really not attached to our life.
It's really a sign that our life is over.
It's outside of ourselves.
It's not a part of our experience.
It's the thing that we don't want to see, that we're hoping will be a long way off.

We see our lives and our deaths as separate events.

It's surprising.
It's a little bit more evident here than it was in my practice before I moved here.
"Now that I feel like I'm 70, vital and 70, my life is behind me now.

Life is right here.
You still have a pulse.
You're still breathing.

You can't have life unless there's death, right?

To live forever is a really big problem.
We're dying all the time, right?
Who you were as a baby is long gone.
The child that you were?
Try and fit into those clothes, huh?
The capability and potential you had as a young adult or a teenager?
Forget it.
I'm never climbing Mount Everest or running another 62 and a quarter miles in 24 hours again in this old body.
Each breath we change.
Each breath we die.
What changes in the moment between life and death is not much really.
It's just the next thing.
How would we know our life if it didn't have an edge?
It's like having endless money or endless things.
You always want more.
There's no end to it.
People in Stanford now, people in Silicon Valley, some of you know this better than I do, they're working on genetics, genome projects so that they can live forever.
That's the new frontier: never having to die.
Forget it.
Think about it.
Even if you could stop the aging process when you're 25, for example, infinite sexual potential, infinite athletic potential, infinite intellectual potential, what would that life be like?
It's like having a plastic flowering arrangement.
It's static.
It's dead.
There's nothing to it.
It has nothing organic to it.
Life is beautiful because it's ephemeral.
Life is beautiful because it's changing, because there's an unknown quality to it, because there are surprises, because there are challenges, and because ultimately it ends.
How could you appreciate the beauty of this life if it were going to go on forever?
It reminds me of when I moved to San Diego for medical school.
I'd been from other parts of the country.
Every day people would get up and say, "It's a beautiful day."
Perfectly blue sky, not a cloud in it.
"It's a beautiful day."
After three days I was like, what do you mean?
So what are we looking for, hoping that we go on forever?
We function in harmony with the world around us by taking our proper place, our proper human place as a human organism, alive and vibrant with all of what that means.
To live within the limit of our life is what gives us life, and that means living out our death.
What's a good life or death?
We think, "Oh, I want to have a good death.
I want to prepare so I have a good death."
Even some of the advance directives, they say, what's your ideal death, right?
Let me write the script.
In the end, what matters is how have I lived my life.
It's impossible to have a good death if you don't live your life out.
That's sad.
So this koan, sun-faced Buddha, moon-faced Buddha.
Sun-faced Buddha means he lives for 108 years, long life, gets to do many things, travel many places, have great experiences, have deep realizations.
Moon-faced Buddha, one day, one night, all done.
Which is better?
Which is better?
It's the one you have, whichever one is Buddha.
Whether you live 108 days or one day, live it completely and you've lived Buddha.
Live 108 years without showing up at all?
I think that's called hell, actually.
I think that's called a big loss.
We can only live in the moment in which we're living.
We can't live all 108 years now.
We can only live this one.
We can live this one fully.
What happens next?
We might say, welcome life.
We might say, as Steve Stuckey, the abbot at San Francisco, said every morning, "Gratitude."
Every morning he'd get up and say, "Gratitude."
The morning after he was diagnosed with terminal pancreatic cancer, he said, "Gratitude."
Or you might say, like my teacher who died 16 years ago, you might say, after a hard swallow, "Andrea, I got some unsettling news.
Great adventure.
What's next?"
A great attitude.
It is a great attitude.
But I think maybe it's even a little bit too much.
I think we don't discriminate good or bad.
We just throw ourselves into the next thing.

Whatever it is, is good."
Whatever it is, is good.
Imagine living with that attitude.
All things are Buddha.
They're neither good nor bad.
They just are Buddha.

This is Katagiri.

The further into practice you go, and you all know this, the more deeply you open to your own suffering, the more deeply you open to the suffering of the world.
You split wide open.
He says, the closer you get to death, suffering and pain do not go away.
Now this isn't one of those heavy Buddhist interpretations.
What he means is, the more you actually open to your life, the more vulnerable you are.

And if you've come close to death or you've had that experience, you know what it's like to open and let go and see that underneath it all, there is this fine, inevitable human experience of suffering, of the loss that we have, of those that we love, of that which we love, the separation, of being in circumstances that are uncomfortable.
We see further and further into that heart and we feel more intimate with it.
We feel it in the quality of our own suffering, like Kisa Gotami learned with the mustard seed, that everyone suffers in this way.
There is no house that has not been touched by death.
And we're so fortunate to have the human mind that cares about such things, that cares about connections, that cares about each other.
So it's inevitable that we have some pain and suffering, of a loss that's a part of the ephemeral nature of life.
We see it in each other.
That's one of the real joys of practicing in sangha over time, knowing each other intimately and opening.
We open ourselves up to each other.
We open up and we get to see people in a deeper way and we understand this fabric that we're all cut out of.

Maybe some of you saw the cartoon that went along with this interview.
It's so moving.
He's very towards the end of his life.
I think he died just a few months after the interview.
He's talking about how he's, whatever he was, 98.
He was very old, and he's lost everyone.
He says this with such tears in his voice and also such joy in his voice.
Everyone's died.
My brother's gone.
All my friends gone.
And really all I do is I sit and look out the window and the trees budding out.
It's blooming.
Life is so beautiful.
I see life is really so beautiful.
That's what Katagiri is talking about.
That is the bittersweet side, the pain and suffering that doesn't go away.
It's the ephemeral nature of everything in our lives.
That's what we come close to as we realize this existence.
It's also the natural part of the life cycle.

When they first moved up to the land there, John had never lived out in the country.
He'd had farms in Berkeley.
He'd had his gardens in Berkeley.
Really nice, sweet man who was a little bit naive about the world.
They moved up when he was in his 60s.
One of the early days he was out in his big garden and there was a dead mole there.
It was so difficult for him.
Maybe you're like him.
I'm a little like him.
"Oh, it's a dead thing.
Oh, it's a dead thing.
How sad.
Oh, isn't this..."

The maggots showed up, then the earthworms, then there was a skeleton, and then there was nothing.
That's how we are.
We're all a part of this cycle of life.
That's how it is.

Another is that there's a feeling of separation.
Isn't that how you sometimes feel when someone dies, that they've left?
But actually, that's a transient thing, I think, that's created by our minds.
After some period of time goes on, if you've lost someone, I bet anyone who has also has a feeling of great intimacy with them in some way.

So he went and he wrote a poem.
He said,

I am going to die.

We all do this.
We all do this.

Oh, that's what this is.
This is how our life goes.
Nothing so special about that.
We think it is because it's our life.
I, me, and mine will no longer exist in the way I'm used to.
Blue Cliff Record, case 55, is Dao Wu's condolence call.
Do you know this one?
The punch line is, Great Teacher Dao Wu and one of his monks have gone off to a funeral.
The coffin is there.
The monk knocks on the coffin.
"Alive or dead?"
"I won't say.
I won't say."
"Teacher, why won't you say?"
"I won't say."
The koan's much more complicated than that, but you basically get that.
Alive or dead.
Some years ago, four years ago, I had the most wonderful dog in the world.
She's 55 pounds and she lived to be 20.
At the very, very end of her life, it was clear, having taken her to the point where she couldn't swallow anymore and she certainly was long past walking, it was time to help her finish her life.
With the vet's permission, I was the one who euthanized her.
I loved that dog dearly and we had had a very physically intimate relationship for the last nine months of her life, carrying her, cleaning her up in the middle of the night, all of that.
When I put the final needle in her and she stopped breathing, it was both like everything changed and nothing had happened at all.
It's so hard to explain that, but it's like that.
Everything changes and nothing happens at all.
Suzuki Roshi likened our lives, our existence, to the waterfall.
Before we're born, we're part of the stream of water.
He saw Yosemite Falls.
If you've ever been there in Yosemite Valley, big fall into a beautiful river.
As the water falls, it breaks up into little droplets that we call Ken and Wayne and John and Marilyn.
And at the bottom, it's the stream again, alive and dead, here or not.

That no matter what, we always exist in the realm of oneness, in the realm of reality.
We have this idea that we have a separate life.
We can't see our death objectively, because we're in the middle of it.
You have to be alive until you're dead.
You can only see death from the perspective of life, usually.
You can't see death from the perspective of death.
Life is all life.
Death is all death.
They don't mix that way.
They're two sides of the same page, but they don't mix.
You can't see death objectively, because you're always outside of it when you're alive.
Our usual way of thinking is to draw distinctions: good or bad, young or old, sick or well.
But our Buddhist life is lived in the midst of all of that.
We just live it.
It's not good or bad.
It's not young or old.
Whatever it is in this moment is what it is.

What would that perspective be like?
What if we could live out all of that reality at once?
Life and death are one piece.
Pick up one side of life, and death will follow along as its opposite.
You can't have one without the other.
They all go along together.
But if you live your life where you are, life is lived.
Death will be lived too.
You and your body will know what to do when the time comes.
You don't have to do anything special.
The supposition is that you'll have a good death if you practice like this.
But you don't know what you're going to get.
You're going to get who you are in that moment under the circumstances.
Just accept it.
Be yourself.

What does he say?
"I don't want to."
That's an honest answer in that moment.
If you look a certain way, you might scream or smile or tremble.
It'll be your karmic manifestation freely expressed.

It happens on its own with forces beyond our conception, so much larger than our own conception.
So much larger.
You can depend on it.
It'll be okay.
It's as miraculous as birth and as ordinary and natural.
When Suzuki Roshi said it's all over, it wasn't a statement of completion or a statement of resignation.
It was a statement of the next thing.
It's it.
It's like saying thusness.
Just it is.
All over, it's everywhere.
Life, death, it's everywhere.
It continues everywhere.

This life, this death, all over, moon reflection and dew drops from the heron's beak collecting back in the pond, manifesting in reality, our lives shaken free for the moment as Kate and Connie and Anne and Bob.
What's the point of preparing for a good death?
It's all around, manifest in this one precious life that each of you is living.
So that's what I have to say.
And I see five minutes, surely you have some response, reaction, objection, question.
Anne.
**Participant:** I just thank you.
Thank you for that.
It's a perfect, absolutely wonderful series.
Beautiful.
**Ryushin Andrea Thach:** Thank you, Anne.
Anything to say about death?
No.
That works.
It always comes right on time.
You heard the talk.
Okay.
Well done.
You're welcome.
